title: Pelvic binder
summary: Binding a suspected broken pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters (the bony points at the top of the outer thighs). TCCC: Combat Medic/Corpsman and Combat Paramedic (pelvic compression device, TCCC skill sets 2024).
indications: TCCC 2026: suspected pelvic fracture after severe blunt force or blast injury, with one or more of the following.
Any major leg amputation or near amputation.
Physical exam findings suggestive of a pelvic fracture (TCCC Combat Lifesaver notes 2025: pelvic deformity or bruising, instability or grating).

JTS CPG 56 (2026) gives a broader indication: severe lower extremity or pelvic injury. JTS CPG 34 (2026) names IED blast, crush and high-velocity penetrating wounds with low blood pressure as high risk (see open questions).
contraindications: The TCCC sources read list no formal contraindication. Their cautions follow.
Do not rock, spring or press the pelvis to test for a fracture: it is a poor test, may dislodge clot and hurts (TCCC proposed change 1602; BSA Wilderness First Aid: avoid rocking the pelvis).
Do not place it at the front points of the hip bones (anterior superior iliac spine): high placement is common and makes it less effective (TCCC proposed change 1602).
Improvised: do not simply tie a single cravat or linked tourniquets around the pelvis; they may not achieve enough tension (TCCC proposed change 1602).
Not under fire or immediate threat (TCCC proposed change 1602: pelvic immobilization is precluded in Care Under Fire).
equipment: A commercial pelvic binder (TCCC proposed change 1602 names cut-to-fit types, the SAM Pelvic Sling and the T-POD; JTS: commercial or SAM-style).

Improvised (TCCC proposed change 1602): a sheet or blanket, or the casualty’s trouser legs, secured with zip ties or clamps; a SAM splint with a CAT tourniquet; or trouser legs cut and tightened with a windlass stick. Improvised methods must be trained and planned in advance.
Tape or cravats to bind the ankles or feet; a rigid litter for carrying.
Two or more people to lift without log-rolling.
complications: Pressure sores from long use or over-tightening (TCCC proposed change 1602). JTS CPG 34 (2026): once on more than 6 hours, check the skin at least every 12 hours; not more than 24 hours if possible.
Placed too high: little effect (TCCC proposed change 1602).
A broken pelvis can bleed heavily inside. Shock that appears or worsens may mean internal bleeding (TCCC skill card 2025).
Theoretical worsening of some fracture patterns; TCCC proposed change 1602 found no clinical evidence of significant harm.

steps.text: Advanced procedure for people trained hands-on to apply a pelvic binder. Have you been trained hands-on to do this?
steps.detail: Reading this is not training. TCCC teaches the pelvic compression device at Combat Medic/Corpsman and Combat Paramedic level (TCCC Skill Sets by Responder Level, 2024). Combat Lifesavers are taught to suspect it and tell medical personnel (CLS notes 2025).

ask.q: Have you been trained hands-on to apply a pelvic binder?

steps.text: Do you have a pelvic binder, or material to improvise one (sheet, blanket, trousers)?
steps.detail: TCCC proposed change 1602: commercial binders, or improvised with a sheet, blanket or trouser legs secured with zip ties or clamps, a SAM splint with a CAT tourniquet, or trouser legs tightened with a windlass stick.

ask.q: Do you have a binder or material to improvise one?

steps.text: Was there a severe blunt or blast injury (a bad fall, crash, crush or explosion)?
steps.detail: TCCC 2026 applies a pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture after severe blunt force or blast injury.

ask.q: Was there a severe blunt or blast injury?

steps.text: Is at least one present: pelvic pain, a leg amputation or near amputation, visible signs of a broken pelvis (see detail), unconsciousness, or shock?
steps.detail:
TCCC 2026 indications: pelvic pain; any major lower limb amputation or near amputation; physical exam findings suggestive of a pelvic fracture; unconsciousness; shock. Signs you can see without pressing: deformity, wounds or bruising near the pelvis (TCCC Combat Lifesaver notes 2025); one leg shorter and turned inward, and bruising between the legs or of the scrotum (JTS CPG 34 2026). TCCC also lists instability or grating; those are found by a trained examiner palpating (CPP skill 2026 step 3), never by rocking or springing the pelvis.

Shock (TCCC): altered mental status without brain injury and/or a weak or absent pulse at the wrist.

Do not rock or press the pelvis to test it.
steps.warn: Do not rock or press the pelvis to test it.

ask.q: Is at least one of these present?

steps.text: Keep them still on their back. Do not log-roll them. Empty their pockets and clear everything from the belt and hips.
steps.detail:
TCCC proposed change 1602: apply the binder before moving the casualty if possible; avoid log-rolling and unnecessary movement; lift gently with two or more people or use a scoop litter. Empty the pockets and remove gear from the belt. Ideally the binder goes on skin, not over clothing.

If a neck or back injury is possible, also follow the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol for how to move them. If they vomit, the airway comes first: Recovery position or Neck or back (spine) injury protocol.

steps.text: Pass the binder under the thighs and slide it up to the greater trochanters (bony bumps at the top of the outer thighs), buckle over the pubic bone. Not at the front points of the hip bones.
steps.detail: TCCC: pass the binder behind the thighs and slide it upward to the level of the greater trochanters, the bony bumps at the top of the outer thighs (skill card 2025). JTS CPG 34 (2026): centred over the greater trochanters with the buckle centred over the pubic symphysis. Proposed change 1602: centre it at the level of the greater trochanters and pubic symphysis, not at the front points of the hip bones (anterior superior iliac spine); placing it too high is common and reduces its effect. If it was passed under the lower back and slid down, check that it sits over the trochanters. Lift gently from behind the back and thighs if needed.
steps.warn: Not at the front points of the hip bones: too high is the common mistake.

steps.text: Commercial binder: pass the strap through the buckle and pull it all the way through, pull the opposing straps until the buckle clicks, keep tension, press the free end down. Improvised: see detail.
steps.detail:
TCCC CPP skill instructions (2026) steps 5 to 7: pass the strap through the buckle and pull it completely through; pull the opposing straps until the buckle clicks (some binders do not click when properly applied); keep the tension and press the free end onto the binder surface. Tighten enough to hold the pelvis, not overtight. Standard: applied in 90 seconds or less.

Improvised (proposed change 1602): sheet, blanket or trouser legs pulled tight and secured with zip ties or clamps, best done by two people, one pulling tight and the other securing. Tighten enough to reduce the fracture without overtightening; it must be wide enough to spread the pressure. Do not simply tie a single cravat or linked tourniquets round the pelvis.

steps.text: Tape or tie the knees and feet together (loosely at the ankles; thighs together if a leg is amputated) so the legs do not roll outward.
steps.detail: JTS CPG 34 (2026): taping the knees and feet together helps hold the legs turned in. TCCC proposed change 1602: loosely strap or tape the ankles or feet together; with an amputation, bind the thighs together; securing the toes prevents the legs rotating outward. TCCC skill card: secure the legs together to minimise outward rotation of the thighs. BSA Wilderness First Aid: secure the legs to each other.

steps.text: Check it: centred over the trochanters and pubic bone, tight but not excessive, skin not pinched. Look for shock.
steps.detail: TCCC proposed change 1602 checks: centred at the trochanters and pubic symphysis, adequate but not excessive tension, ankles or thighs secured, skin checked for pressure injury. TCCC skill card: assess for shock, which may mean internal bleeding.

ask.q: Are there signs of shock, or are they getting worse?

steps.text: Shock: recheck the binder position and tightness and reapply it if needed. Use the Shock protocol and evacuate immediately.
steps.detail: TCCC skill card (2025): reapply the binder if signs of shock appear or worsen. A binder does not rule out a junctional tourniquet if one is needed. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Keep them lying still and warm. Carry them on a rigid litter. Recheck the binder, their skin and signs of shock often. Evacuate urgently.
steps.detail:
Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

BSA Wilderness First Aid: secure the whole person on a rigid litter before carrying them out, and watch for shock from internal bleeding. Keep them warm (Shock protocol).

JTS CPG 34 (2026): if a binder has been on for more than 6 hours, the skin under it is checked at least every 12 hours, holding the pelvis reduced while the binder is taken down and reapplied, and binders or sheets should not be left in place for more than 24 hours if possible. The app’s caution: those skin checks are for medical personnel; do not loosen or remove the binder yourself in the field; evacuate so this can be done by medical personnel (see open questions).

steps.text: Do not apply a tight binder. If you have or can find a wide sheet or blanket, you may tie it snugly around the hips for support. Keep them still, rigid litter, evacuate urgently.
steps.detail: American Red Cross Wilderness and Remote First Aid (2014, p. 36): place wide conforming wraps, such as a sheet or blanket, and tie them around the pelvis to give some support and security; secure the person on a rigid litter before a carry-out; watch for shock. BSA Wilderness First Aid: conforming wraps give support, and the legs can be secured to each other. Do not rock or press the pelvis. The Broken bone (fracture) protocol covers keeping them still. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: TCCC’s trigger for a binder is not met. Use the Broken bone (fracture) protocol and watch for shock.
steps.detail: TCCC 2026 applies a binder after severe blunt force or blast injury with pelvic pain, a leg amputation, signs of fracture, unconsciousness or shock. If any of these appear later, come back here.

donts: Do not rock, spring or press the pelvis to test it.
Do not put the binder at the front points of the hip bones; it goes at the greater trochanters.
Do not log-roll a casualty with a suspected broken pelvis; lift with two or more people.
Do not overtighten, and do not use a single cravat or linked tourniquets as a binder.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently every casualty with a suspected broken pelvis, on a rigid litter.
Most urgent: signs of shock, unconsciousness, or a leg amputation.
